entries.reason: The same argument with a fixed suffix appended, in the same maintainer-only tool. The suffix is written here rather than taken as a second flag precisely so the two names are decided in one place: a signer and a verifier that disagree about where the signature lives is a failure nobody sees until an install is refused.

The manifest path is this tool's own -manifest argument, typed by whoever is publishing a release - the same argument as the two -sign/-verify entries above and the same tool. cmd/releasesign is the maintainer's, not the product's: it is kept out of the release package by notShipped in release/release_test.go, no service invokes it, and it has no network surface. A tool asked to sign the file it was named cannot refuse to open it.

The path is this tool's own -sign/-verify argument, typed by whoever is building a release. cmd/releasesign is the maintainer's tool: it is not in the release package (see notShipped in release/release_test.go), no service invokes it, and it has no network surface at all - the only caller is a person at a terminal and release/build.sh. A tool whose whole job is 'sign the file I name' cannot refuse to open the file it was named.

0644 is deliberate and 0600 would be the bug. This file is an Ed25519 signature over SHA256SUMS - public by construction, and useless if the person who unpacks the package cannot read it. It carries no secret: the signing key never leaves the maintainer's environment (CA_RELEASE_KEY) and is not derivable from a signature. Every other file in the package is world-readable for the same reason, and a signature nobody can read verifies nothing.

The conversion is guarded on the line above it. blocksToBytes refuses any block count that would overflow - `blocks > MaxInt64/unit` - and returns MaxInt64 instead, so int64(blocks) is reached only for values that fit. Saturating rather than wrapping is deliberate: the number is bytes free on a disk, it is read off a health page, and a negative figure there is worse than one stuck at the maximum. It needs a filesystem of nine exabytes to reach either. gosec sees the conversion and not the bound three lines up.
Truncation is the operation, not an accident: GREASE detection compares the high and low bytes of a uint16 (RFC 8701), so byte(v) is deliberate.

G101 matches on the identifier name, not on the value. DiagBadCredentials is a diagnosis key the panel looks up a Turkish sentence by, and "kimlik_reddedildi" is that key - it is never compared against anything, stored, or sent. Renaming the constant to slip past the rule would replace the clearest name in the file with a worse one to please a scanner.

G101 matches the identifier name, not the value. mailPasswordLabel is the additional authenticated data binding a sealed value to the panel_smtp.password column - it is deliberately not secret, it is documented as not secret in internal/sealed, and its whole job is to be a fixed public string that a value from another column will not authenticate against. Third finding of this shape in the repository: a product whose subject matter is credentials names things after credentials, and G101 reads names.

The signature beside the list, same fixed name, same root. The suffix is appended here rather than configured so the signer and the verifier cannot disagree about where a signature lives. This is an unpacker: reading a path it computed is what the function does, and gosec cannot see the check in front of it. What bounds the path is safeJoin, which refuses any ".." element outright rather than cleaning one away, refuses absolute paths and NUL bytes, and then checks the joined result is still under the root - two walls, because a single check in front of a path join is one too few when the consequence is a file where systemd looks. Measured rather than argued: TestEveryHostilePackageIsRefused covers climbing paths, absolute paths, symlinks, hard links and device nodes, TestNothingIsWrittenOutsideTheDirectoryEvenOnRefusal checks the disk rather than the return value (refusing after writing is not refusing), and FuzzUnpackNeverEscapesItsDirectory ran 644,598 archives without one entry appearing beside the unpack directory.

The installation's bin directory, which four services running as a different account must be able to enter and execute out of. 0750 would work only while the group happens to be right and breaks the moment it is not; install.sh creates the same directory with the same mode. This is not the unpack tree - that one is 0700, because nothing but the upgrader has any business in it until verification passes.

0755 is required here and 0600 would be the bug. These are the service binaries: systemd runs them as the `crucible` account, and this code runs as `crucible-upgrader`. A binary installed 0600 is a binary its own service cannot execute, and the symptom is status=203/EXEC on every unit - the exact failure U1 was written to close. install.sh installs the same files with the same mode for the same reason, and TestAGoodPackageReplacesTheBinaries asserts the executable bit survives. The Chmod repeats the mode after the write because OpenFile's permission argument is masked by umask, and an upgrader running under umask 077 would otherwise install binaries nothing can run.

Writing the new binary beside its destination before renaming it into place. The path is the destination this Installer was configured with, joined to a file name read out of the unpacked package's bin/ directory - and that package has already been fetched over https, unpacked with every hostile shape refused, verified against our Ed25519 signature, and verified file by file against its own SHA256SUMS. Nothing from the request row reaches any of it: the row carries a version, whose shape relupdate.ValidVersion checks, and the address is built from upgrader.toml. Written-then-renamed rather than written in place because Linux refuses to write to a running executable (ETXTBSY) and rename(2) over an open file is fine.

The nil is required, not hardcoded. cipher.NewGCMWithRandomNonce returns an AEAD that draws its own nonce - crypto/internal/fips140/aes/gcm calls drbg.Read(nonce) - and panics on any nonce handed to it ("non-empty nonce passed to GCMWithRandomNonce"). That construction was chosen precisely because it makes nonce reuse unreachable, which is how GCM actually fails in the field. Verified against the Go 1.25 source and by TestSealIsNotDeterministic, which seals the same plaintext fifty times and gets fifty different ciphertexts.
